golden-gate.name: Golden Gate
golden-gate.overview: The gilded entrance in the royal palace frontage leads toward the palace courtyards and the Taleju sanctuary. It is distinct from Khauma, the western entrance to the square.
golden-gate.history: Cambridge Museums describes the gate as begun under Bhupatindra Malla and completed under Ranjit Malla in 1754. Tourism Board publications differ between 1753 and 1754; the completion year is therefore not treated as uncontested.
golden-gate.architecture: Gilded copper ornament contrasts with the surrounding red brick. The torana includes Garuda and a multi-headed, multi-armed representation of Taleju; inscriptions flank the portal. The metalwork frames a ceremonial threshold rather than a freestanding city gate.
golden-gate.significance: The gate expresses the relationship between Malla kingship, the royal palace and Taleju. Its religious setting should not be confused with unrestricted public access to every inner court.

fifty-five-frontage.name: Fifty-Five Window Palace
fifty-five-frontage.overview: The palace is distinguished by its continuous carved timber window gallery. It is part of the royal complex but has a history separate from the Golden Gate and the museum wing.
fifty-five-frontage.history: The 2006 conservation report dates construction to 1702-1722 under Bhupatindra Malla and notes an attribution of the foundations to Jitamitra Malla. NTB describes a 15th-century palace origin. These accounts are not assumed to date the same surviving fabric. The 1934 earthquake badly damaged the window gallery, which was rebuilt using salvaged timbers with changes to its projecting support.
fifty-five-frontage.architecture: Brick masonry, carved timber windows and structural frames, tiled roofs and painted interiors form a layered palace architecture. The conservation report records traditional ma appa and dachi appa brickwork with mud mortar, and first-floor murals including a Shiva Visvarupa composition.
fifty-five-frontage.significance: The royal residence preserves evidence of Malla court culture and Newar timber craftsmanship. Its murals and window gallery preserve distinct artistic traditions within the same royal building.

gallery-frontage.name: National Art Gallery
gallery-frontage.overview: The National Art Gallery occupies part of Bhaktapur's former royal palace. It is distinct from the Fifty-Five Window Palace farther east along the frontage.
gallery-frontage.history: NTB dates the museum's establishment to 1960 under the Department of Archaeology. The palace wing is older: local accounts associate its lion entrance with Simhadhwaka Durbar. The Department of Archaeology's 2022 report documents conservation of the western gallery wing after the 2015 earthquake, using lime-based masonry work and Sal timber.
gallery-frontage.architecture: The brick entrance has carved timber openings and prominent guardian sculpture. The adjoining white, Rana-period remodelled frontage is architecturally distinct. The local name of the lion-gate palace must not be applied indiscriminately to every section of the modern museum complex.
gallery-frontage.significance: The museum preserves painting, manuscripts and stone sculpture associated with Hindu and Buddhist traditions. NTB highlights paubha painting among its collections. The historical palace building and the museum institution therefore have different chronologies.

gopinath-krishna.name: Gopinath Temple
gopinath-krishna.overview: This two-roof temple belongs to the western Durbar Square entrance cluster. The Department of Archaeology identifies Gopi Nath with Dwarika or Krishna Temple; the local Radhakrishna name is also documented.
gopinath-krishna.history: The 2015 earthquake damaged the sanctum walls. DoA records shoring, replacement of deteriorated ground-floor Sal timber and use of lime mortar in conservation. Its 2022 report describes repair without wholesale dismantling, with the project completed in fiscal year 2076-77 BS. These reports do not establish an original construction year or patron.
gopinath-krishna.architecture: The documented form is a two-roof Nepalese temple with brick masonry and important structural timber. Photographs show a broad lower roof, a smaller upper roof and carved timber entrance work.
gopinath-krishna.significance: The temple is dedicated to Krishna. DoA lists Satyabhama, Krishna and Radha in its sanctum, while a local account supplies a different accompanying deity list. The Krishna dedication is secure; the conflicting subsidiary identifications are not silently merged.

vatsala-durga.name: Vatsala Durga Temple
vatsala-durga.overview: Vatsala Durga is the stone shikhara temple in the central palace forecourt. Its Durga dedication and three-stage plinth are documented by the Department of Archaeology. It is distinct from the nearby two-roof Yaksheshwar temple and from other Vatsala-named shrines.
vatsala-durga.history: DoA gives an initial construction under Jitamitra Malla in 1696 and rebuilding under Bhupatindra Malla around the turn of the 18th century. A local account instead gives 1672 and 1674. The 2015 earthquake destroyed the temple. Foundation investigations involved DoA, UNESCO and Durham University, followed by municipal reconstruction on the retained foundation. The 2019 report describes work still in progress.
vatsala-durga.architecture: The sandstone temple combines a substantial stepped base, axial stairs, guardians and a deeply articulated lower level beneath a tapering shikhara. Secondary projections, niches, cornices and an ornamental crown break up the stone tower. The licensed 2026 photograph documents the standing rebuilt form rather than proving an exact completion date.
vatsala-durga.significance: Its dedication to Durga places the shrine within the palace square's religious ensemble. The reconstructed building also records the substantial conservation response to the 2015 earthquake.

large-bell.name: Taleju Bell
large-bell.overview: The large bell is a separate assembly in the royal forecourt near the Golden Gate and Fifty-Five Window Palace. It must not be confused with the smaller bell beside Vatsala.
large-bell.history: NTB's Cultural Treasures publication and the local bell account attribute the large bell to Ranjit Malla in 1737. The local account reports an inscription date of 6 January, but that precise day has not been independently checked against an epigraphic transcription.
large-bell.architecture: A substantial hanging metal bell is carried on an independent raised support assembly. The 2015 photograph shows its scale and separation from the pavilion and palace. This image includes earthquake damage elsewhere in the forecourt and must not be read as a present-day view.
large-bell.significance: The documented bell is associated with worship of Taleju, the royal protective goddess. No modern ringing schedule or visitor access practice is asserted here.

malla-column.name: Bhupatindra Malla Column
malla-column.period: Malla royal monument; installation year unresolved
malla-column.overview: A seated royal figure rises above the plaza on a slender stone column. The documented identification is King Bhupatindra Malla, shown with joined hands facing toward the Golden Gate and Taleju precinct.
malla-column.history: A local heritage account interprets the column as an expression of Bhupatindra Malla's royal devotion. The consulted evidence does not securely establish an installation year, so no exact year or unsupported story about damage is presented.
malla-column.architecture: The stone shaft supports a broad ornamented lotus-like capital and a seated metal figure. The folded legs, joined hands, seat, thin supporting pole and parasol are important parts of its silhouette. The licensed close photograph is the primary evidence for these visible details.
malla-column.significance: The ruler's prayerful posture connects royal authority with devotion to Taleju. The column is a forecourt monument, not a temple and not a generic decorative pillar.

chyasilin.name: Chyasilin Mandap
chyasilin.period: Historical pavilion; modern reconstruction project from 1987
chyasilin.overview: Chyasilin is the octagonal pavilion beside the palace forecourt. Its present form is a documented modern reconstruction of the pavilion lost in the 1934 earthquake, not wholly surviving Malla-period fabric.
chyasilin.history: The reconstruction account describes royal reception and festival viewing, an inscribed record of a poetry competition, and later use as a tax office. After the 1934 collapse, a reconstruction was proposed in 1987 by Götz Hagmüller and Niels Gutschow. Historic photographs and surviving carved posts informed the design. Dated 1990 bolt heads identify the modern intervention; the authors report that the pavilion survived the 2015 earthquake without damage.
chyasilin.architecture: Two roofs cover an octagonal timber pavilion. Traditional carved elements coexist with modern steel trusses, foundations and an inner supporting system. That structural distinction is explicitly described by the reconstruction authors. The two included photographs show lower carved posts and the whole pavilion in the forecourt.
chyasilin.significance: The pavilion served royal and public viewing functions and is an important example of an openly documented reconstruction. Its survival in 2015 should be understood alongside its modern structural reinforcement.

khauma-gate.name: Khauma Gate
khauma-gate.overview: Khauma is the principal western entrance gate to Bhaktapur Durbar Square. Its city-entry role is distinct from the gilded Golden Gate in the royal palace frontage.
khauma-gate.history: DoA records collapse of the southern portion and cracking of upper masonry in the 2015 earthquake. Damaged work was dismantled down to the foundations and restored using traditional techniques, including Sal posts and timber ties. The consulted report does not establish the gate's original date or patron.
khauma-gate.architecture: The entrance is a masonry gateway with a pointed central opening, articulated side masses and an ornamental curved crown. These visible forms are documented by the licensed photograph.
khauma-gate.significance: The gateway marks the transition from the western streets into the heritage square. Its post-earthquake repair is documented independently of the more elaborate royal Golden Gate.

yaksheshwar.name: Yaksheshwar Temple
yaksheshwar.overview: This two-roof Shiva temple stands south of Vatsala in the central square. DoA identifies Yakshyashwor as a 15th-century monument; local documentation also calls it Pashupatinath. It is not the similarly named Kathmandu temple complex.
yaksheshwar.history: The 2022 DoA report records partial damage in the 2015 earthquake and conservation without wholesale dismantling, still under way at the time of reporting. Local accounts associate the temple with Yaksha Malla, but their precise 1475 date is not treated as independently established.
yaksheshwar.architecture: Two spreading tiled roofs shelter a brick and carved-timber temple. Carved struts and entrance work are important parts of its Shaiva imagery. The included post-earthquake photograph locates it beside the then-damaged Vatsala site.
yaksheshwar.significance: The Shiva/Pashupati dedication belongs to Bhaktapur's own religious landscape. Shared divine names do not make its history interchangeable with Kathmandu's Pashupatinath.

siddhi-lakshmi.name: Siddhi Lakshmi Temple
siddhi-lakshmi.overview: The stone shikhara temple near the southeastern side of the Fifty-Five Window Palace is identified by DoA as Siddhi Lakshmi. Its elevated stair approach and paired guardians distinguish it from the nearby brick shikhara.
siddhi-lakshmi.history: DoA dates the temple to the 17th century. It was damaged, but did not collapse, in 2015. Conservation retained the foundation and plinth, numbered and reused dismantled stone elements, and renewed damaged timber structure and the gilded pinnacle.
siddhi-lakshmi.architecture: An axial staircase climbs a high stepped plinth to a compact stone shikhara. Paired sculptural guardians flank successive levels of the approach. Moulded courses and a crowned tapering tower give the stone mass a strong vertical silhouette.
siddhi-lakshmi.significance: The temple is dedicated to Siddhi Lakshmi. Its repaired fabric illustrates a conservation approach that retained the historic base and reused identifiable stone members rather than treating the whole monument as a new replica.

silu-mahadev.name: Silu Mahadev Temple
silu-mahadev.period: Historic Shiva shrine; present form reconstructed
silu-mahadev.overview: Silu Mahadev, also called Fasi Dega, is the tall Shiva temple on the monumental stepped base at the eastern end of the square. It is distinguished by its broad, stepped-plinth site and restored tower.
silu-mahadev.history: The 1934 earthquake damaged the earlier temple; a dome-roofed replacement subsequently occupied the surviving stepped base. The 2015 earthquake destroyed that upper building. DoA's 2022 report describes reconstruction of the pre-1934 form in its final phase. The licensed 2024 photograph shows the standing rebuilt temple, without establishing a precise completion day.
silu-mahadev.architecture: Six substantial plinth stages carry a tall, articulated brick shikhara. The broad stair-and-platform composition is central to its identity and contrasts with the former dome-roofed replacement described in the conservation reports.
silu-mahadev.significance: The Shiva dedication and the recovery of a pre-1934 architectural form connect the site's religious continuity with repeated earthquake reconstruction. The present superstructure is not described as untouched original fabric.
